documents.citation: W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk, Chapter I, 1903. Library of Congress and Project Gutenberg.
documents.excerpt: After the Egyptian and Indian, the Greek and Roman, the Teuton and Mongolian, the Negro is a sort of seventh son, born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world — a world which yields him no true self-consciousness, but only lets him see himself through the revelation of the other world. It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity. One ever feels his two-ness — an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder.

documents.citation: Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified August 18, 1920. National Archives, Washington, D.C.
documents.excerpt: The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex. Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation.

documents.citation: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House, Chapter XI, 1910. Library of Congress and Project Gutenberg.
documents.excerpt: We were constantly told by our neighbors that the women of the Hull-House group should be able to understand the workingman's point of view because we ourselves were in the position of a disenfranchised class and knew what it meant to stand outside and look in. The settlement in its first years was identified with the labor movement as one of the bodies which also believed that the ballot was not an end in itself but that the vote must be followed by a genuine sense of civic responsibility.
